chunks: From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Fadalah, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When a man swears an oath regarding something, and the doing of that thing is better than leaving it, then he should do that which is better and there is no expiation (kaffarah) upon him, and that is from the paces of Satan.
ai.seo_question: Do I need to pay expiation (kaffarah) if I swear to do something good?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, clarifying that when the sworn action is inherently superior to its omission, fulfillment suffices without expiation, distinguishing it from general oaths. The attribution to 'the paces of Satan' reflects the Shia scholarly view that such oaths often arise from minor distractions or hesitation rather than deliberate sin, thereby mitigating the need for *kaffarah*. This highlights the juristic principle of prioritizing the substantive good of the act over the formal rigidity of the oath when the intent is beneficial.
